title: Women Hold Just 11% of Management Jobs in Japan
paragraphs: In 2020, the Japanese government said it wanted women to hold around 30% of leadership positions before the end of the decade.
Six years later, however, many companies are still far from that goal.

A survey by Teikoku Databank looked at more than 22,000 companies across Japan in July this year. At these companies, women now hold only 11.3% of management positions — just 0.2 percentage points more than last year.
And at 42% of companies, every manager is a man.
It's a similar story for executives. Women now make up 14.2% of executives, a 0.4 percentage point increase from last year. And more than half of companies have no female executives at all.
Still, many companies believe these numbers will change. Eleven percent think the number of female executives will increase, and 30% expect to have more female managers in the future.
Among companies with more than 1,000 workers, 73% expect to have more female managers.

The Japanese government has introduced rules to try to help bring more women into senior jobs. Since 2022, companies with more than 100 workers have had to make action plans to support women at work, and publish information about their progress.
The rules were expanded in April 2026, and these companies must now also publish information such as the percentage of their managers who are women, and the difference in pay between men and women.

So there are signs that more women could move into management, especially at larger companies. But with women still holding only about 11% of management positions, Japan remains a long way from the government's 30% goal.
